Beat. The underlying regular pulse in music, the steady, recurring pulse that listeners can feel and musicians align to. Distinct from the complexity of rhythm, the beat is the simplest periodic reference point that organizes musical time. It is the physical anchor that dancers respond to, the pulse audiences tap their feet to, and the temporal reference all other rhythmic events relate to.

The beat is the fundamental periodic pulse, typically sensed as a steady one-two-three-four or similar recurring pattern. Beats are grouped into larger units by meter, and the interaction of beat and meter creates the perceived temporal structure. A tempo indication specifies how fast the beat occurs, for example, quarter note equals one hundred twenty beats per minute. Syncopation is meaningful only because it defines melodic or harmonic events that fall off the beat for expressive displacement.

In ensemble playing, all musicians align to a common beat, making it the essential shared reference for ensemble coordination. The beat is not the same as the downbeat, the first beat of a measure, which is a beat with metrical emphasis. Listeners naturally internalize and motor-synchronize to the beat, even when it is not explicitly sounded. In conducting, the conductor marks the beat with hand gestures, and ensemble musicians watch the conductor to maintain synchronization with a common temporal reference.

The beat can be subdivided into smaller note values like eighth notes or sixteenth notes for purposes of rhythmic precision and performance control. Musicians develop an internalized sense of the beat through practice and ear training. Feeling the beat is essential to expressive performance and ensemble cohesion. Different musical styles emphasize the beat differently. Rock and pop music tend to emphasize beats two and four, called the backbeat, while classical music emphasizes beat one, the downbeat.

In dance, the beat directly corresponds to step patterns. Dancers count beats to synchronize with music, making the beat the physical anchor for choreography. Entrainment, the tendency for humans and animals to synchronize motor movements to external rhythms, is strongest to a steady, clear beat, explaining why audiences move, nod, or tap to music. The beat connects to rhythm as the most fundamental component, meter as the organizing principle, tempo as the speed, syncopation as creating expressive interest, and polyrhythm as overlaying multiple patterns.
